newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK October output prices to stay subdued.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK October output prices to stay subdued.

text.p: Lower commodity and raw material import prices should have offset the impact of higher oil prices in October, ensuring British factory gate prices remained subdued, analysts said on Friday.
The Reuters consensus forecast is for output prices to have risen 0.2 percent in October on the previous month, giving a 2.3 percent annual rise compared with September's 2.2 percent rate.
Input prices are likely to have risen 0.2 percent month-on-month, giving an annual rate of -2.0 percent, versus -2.9 percent last month. The data are due at 0930 GMT on Monday.

With growing consumer demand tempting retailers to widen margins and pass on modest cost increases to high street shoppers, analysts said the jumpy gilt market may take small comfort from benign data.
"October presents a similar picture to September of firmer oil prices, but lower commodity prices overall," said Union Discount group economist Philip Shaw.
"Also, sterling's trade weighted index rose by 2.5 percent over the period, the sharpest rise since mid-1993, putting downward pressure on the cost of imported non-commodity inputs."

Jonathan Loynes from HSBC Markets said its in-house commodity index fell by around one percent in October from September's average level, as further rises in fuel costs were more than offset by falls in other commodities such as metals, chemicals and food.
"This index follows a close relationship with unadjusted input prices on a monthly basis," he said, adding he expected seasonally adjusted input prices to fall by around 0.4 percent in October.
With core producer price inflation dipping to a 30-year low of 0.9 percent in September, economists noted the good news on British factory gate prices may soon be over.
"The core output price index is either at the bottom or extremely close to it now," said Bank of America economist Jeremy Hawkins.
Even at these levels, UK retail prices have remained stubbornly high, with the underlying inflation rate refusing to fall below 2.8 percent.
"At the end of the day, retailers have chosen not to feed weak producer prices through," said BZW economist David Hillier.

Economists said that while intense competitive pressure on the high street was keeping a lid on prices rises at present, a sustained pick up in consumer demand would soon allow retailers to pass on costs and widen margins.
"Risks will clearly start to build that we'll start to see an increase in profit margins coming through," Hawkins said.
"But most evidence is still that where demand has risen it's been due to weakness in prices -- prices are leading demand higher, it's not strong demand leading prices."
Hillier said that with manufacturing productivity coming back strongly, offsetting unit wage cost growth, the need for margins to rise may diminish.
Daiwa economist Katy Peters said that with the best news on producer prices over, inflation risks were on the upside.

"Now we've got the end of the good news on producer prices and consumer demand is strengthening, suggesting the widening of margins will continue, if not increase. It's bad news for inflation," she said.
Hawkins said the figures would provide the gilt and short sterling markets with little excuse to outperform.

"So long as we see no significant deterioration in the data, we should be all right. But the real problem is the market is blinkered. There's a bias towards looking for bad news, so if the data are weaker, there won't be much improvement in gilts or short sterling," he said.
